Yongtai Palace.name: Yongtai Palace
Yongtai Palace.basicInfo: The seat of House Yongtai and the political center of Qianzhou, standing at the heart of Wanhua just north of the Garrison. Its south approach is the city's most formal space — wide, ceremonial, heavily watched — while its northern reaches, reserved for the imperial family and those closest to them, are quiet, guarded, and largely closed to outsiders.

South Main Gate.description: The Palace's formal entrance, facing the Garrison across a stretch of open ground kept deliberately clear of stalls or clutter. Guards in full ceremonial dress flank the gate day and night, though their real vigilance is more visible in how they watch approaching palanquins than in their posture. Petitioners without an appointment wait here, sometimes for hours.

North Gate.description: A smaller, unadorned service gate on the Palace's northern wall, used for deliveries, staff, and anyone whose business doesn't require the formality of the south approach. Carts of provisions and firewood pass through here daily, checked by guards far less concerned with ceremony than ability to recognize a familiar face.

Imperial Way.description: A wide ceremonial path running straight from South Main Gate to Fengming Hall, paved in fitted stone and flanked by nothing that would obstruct a clear line of sight down its length. Officials and petitioners cross it on foot, heads slightly bowed by unspoken custom even when no one of rank is actually present to see it.

Fengming Hall.description: The throne hall, and the Palace's true center — a vast chamber where the ruling Emperor or Empress hears petitions, issues verdicts, and receives visiting dignitaries. Lacquered pillars rise to a coffered ceiling, and the throne itself sits raised on a dais, positioned so that anyone approaching must cross the entire length of the room to be heard.

Administration Wing.description: The Palace's working bureaucratic heart, folded in near the south approach rather than the private quarters — clerks, tax records, and the household's day-to-day administrative business run through here. Stacks of paper and the low murmur of officials reading aloud to each other replace the ceremony of the halls beyond it.

Palace Gardens.description: Landscaped grounds behind Fengming Hall, offering the closest thing to privacy the Palace's public wings allow — ornamental ponds, covered walkways, and plantings chosen as much for symbolic meaning as beauty. Officials granted a private audience are sometimes walked here rather than received in the hall, a subtle signal of favor.

Performance Pavilion.description: An open-sided pavilion near Fengming Hall where musicians, dancers, and performers entertain the court on festival days and during formal receptions. Instruments and staging are kept ready year-round, since a visiting dignitary or a sudden change of mood in the ruler can call for entertainment on short notice.

Neiyuan.description: The private residence of the ruling family, set apart from the Palace's public wings by both distance and guarded access. Modest in scale compared to Fengming Hall's grandeur, its rooms are furnished for daily life rather than display — the one part of the Palace where the ruler is not, technically, on display.

Attendants' Quarters.description: Housing for the household staff, stewards, and personal attendants who work closest to the imperial family — separate from ordinary servant lodging elsewhere in the city, and granted for the trust the work itself requires. Simple, close, and quiet, with an unusual amount of coming and going at odd hours.

Watchtowers.description: Elevated posts along the Palace's outer wall, manned in rotating shifts day and night, giving clear sightlines over both the south approach and the service gate. From here the Garrison's drill yard is visible in the distance, a reminder that the Palace's actual protection sits just beyond its own walls.

Yongtai Palace.hiddenInfo:
The Palace's public face is one of undivided authority beneath the ruler — but the heir has spent years quietly building something the ruler doesn't fully see. Through private correspondence and money that never passes through official channels, the heir has cultivated real personal loyalty with the garrison commanders at Ningyao and Chengyuan — loyalty strong enough that those circuits would likely follow the heir's word over the throne's, if it ever came to it. The ruler still believes those garrisons are held the usual way: through the Palace's own enforcement, not anyone's private network.

The heir's own eunuch steward, who manages the heir's household finances, has been quietly diverting resources to fund this — small enough to escape notice, but real and ongoing. A sharp clerk cross-referencing the right ledgers could catch the irregularity, though not its actual purpose.
The heir isn't moving yet, and won't until the ruler's position looks genuinely vulnerable. Until then, this is patience, not rebellion — every outward appearance stays loyal.

Garrison.name: Garrison
Garrison.basicInfo: A walled barracks and staging ground immediately south of Yongtai Palace, positioned as the physical buffer between the Palace's own approach and the rest of the city. Soldiers drill in its yard in full view of anyone passing between the Market District and the Park, a deliberate, visible reminder of House Yongtai's authority.
Garrison.hiddenInfo: This garrison houses the core of House Yongtai's standing military. Drill here is genuinely rigorous in appearance — formation marching, weapons practice, visible discipline — but none of it has been tested in a real engagement in three generations. For years, senior officers here have quietly inflated the readiness reports sent up to the Palace, a practice each generation of commanders inherited rather than started, too afraid of the ruler's temper to report the truth. A newly appointed inspector, not yet part of the arrangement, has been asking pointed questions here, and several officers have grown visibly on edge since. A soldier or officer stationed here who talks too freely, especially after drink, is a real and plausible way this secret could start to unravel.

Pagoda Area.name: Pagoda Area
Pagoda Area.basicInfo: A tiered pagoda rising beside the Suining River between the Grand Bridge and the Entertainment District, serving as teahouse, viewing tower, and the city's passenger boat landing all at once. By day it draws travelers waiting on a ferry and locals climbing for the view; by night its upper tiers catch the same lantern light as the Entertainment District beyond it.

Ground Floor Teahouse.description: The pagoda's base level, given over to low tables and a working kitchen serving tea and simple food to travelers and boat passengers waiting on the next crossing. Steam and the smell of broth drift out toward the riverside path. Porters and ferry-goers set down bags here rather than carry them up the stairs, so the floor stays cluttered with baggage no one quite watches closely.

Viewing Tier.description: The pagoda's upper tier, open on all four sides, reached by a narrow staircase that discourages casual crowding. From here the Suining, the Grand Bridge, and the lantern-lit edge of the Entertainment District are all visible at once. A favored spot for quiet conversation precisely because climbing the stairs filters out anyone not willing to make the effort.

Ferry Landing.description: A wooden landing at the pagoda's river-facing side where passenger boats take on and set down travelers along the Suining. No cargo moves through here — this is people only, unlike the overland routes that carry Wanhua's actual trade. Boatmen call out departures over the water, and the landing stays busy with arrivals timed around the pagoda's meal hours.

Pagoda Area.hiddenInfo: Because the landing handles only passengers and never cargo, it draws far less scrutiny from tax clerks and garrison patrols than the Market District's overland routes do — a gap a few boatmen have quietly learned to use. Letters and small, easily-hidden items occasionally travel by passenger rather than by official courier, changing hands in the crowded baggage clutter at the Ground Floor Teahouse where no one is watching any particular bag. This isn't organized smuggling. No one currently organizes or controls this informal network — a real opening for someone willing to formalize it into something bigger: a proper courier service, a trade concern, or something greyer, entirely built from what's currently just a handful of boatmen doing favors.

Grand Bridge.name: Grand Bridge
Grand Bridge.basicInfo: A wide stone bridge spanning the Suining River, the single most prominent crossing in Wanhua, connecting the Market District to the Entertainment District. Vendors and stalls line its length year-round, and during festivals it becomes the city's most crowded gathering point — lanterns strung end to end, performers competing for space, and foot traffic slowing to a crawl. Locally regarded as the heart of the city as much as the Palace itself.

Entertainment District.name: Entertainment District
Entertainment District.basicInfo: Wanhua's lantern-lit night quarter east of the Palace, reached by the Grand Bridge — home to the Xiangpu Arena, dozens of wine houses and food stalls along Lantern Row, and Ruanxiang Yuan, the district's most prominent pleasure house. By day it is quiet and half-asleep; by night it is the loudest, most crowded part of the city.

Grand Bridge Approach.description: The threshold where the Grand Bridge empties into the Entertainment District. The first lanterns and food stalls appear here, and the noise of Lantern Row builds gradually as the crowd thickens with every step deeper in. A natural place to linger, get bearings, or wait for someone before committing further into the district.

Lantern Row.description: The district's main strip, packed with minor wine houses, food stalls, and street performers competing for coin — opera singers, storytellers, acrobats. Old men bend over weiqi boards outside teahouses, oblivious to the noise around them. Lantern light replaces daylight entirely after dusk, and the crowd rarely thins before the small hours.

Xiangpu Arena.description: A sunken ring surrounded by tiered wooden seating, host to marketplace-tier xiangpu bouts most nights and occasional court-attended matches on festival days. Wrestlers of both sexes compete here, a real and unremarkable feature of the sport rather than a novelty. The air carries sweat, dust, and the roar of a crowd placing side bets between rounds.

Chunfeng.description: The most prominent wine house on Lantern Row, distinct from the anonymous stalls around it — private rooms, better wine, and a clientele of merchants entertaining contacts and minor officials relaxing off the record. Real business and real gossip both change hands here, often over the same cup. Discretion is part of what patrons are paying for.

Ruanxiang Yuan.description: The Entertainment District's most prominent building, a multi-story pleasure house where courtesans are valued first for genuine artistic skill — guqin, pipa, dance, poetry, conversation — with companionship as one part of a broader, real institution rather than its entirety. Reception halls host formal entertaining; private rooms are separate and unremarked upon. Treated as a normal, established part of the city's social fabric, not a scandal.

Market District.name: Market District
Market District.basicInfo: Wanhua's commercial heart, stretching south and southeast of Yongtai Palace, past the Garrison. Dense stalls, workshops, and vendors packed shoulder to shoulder, with constant foot, horse, and palanquin traffic from dawn well into the evening. The largest and busiest concentration of ordinary daily life in the city.

North Residential District.name: North Residential District
North Residential District.basicInfo: A residential quarter north of Yongtai Palace, home to a mix of ordinary households, minor officials, and established local families. Quieter and more orderly than the Market District, with its own small shops and gathering spots serving residents rather than travelers.

West Residential District.name: West Residential District
West Residential District.basicInfo: A residential quarter west of Yongtai Palace, river- and park-adjacent, connected to the Park by a footbridge over the Suining. Generally more affluent than the North Residential District, favored by households wanting proximity to the Park's quiet without living inside the Palace's immediate shadow.

Zhenhai Camp.name: Zhenhai Camp
Zhenhai Camp.basicInfo: Zhenhai Camp, Suwei Ying's central garrison in Ningyao, sits inland from both the coast and the circuit's northern highlands — a deliberate position, close enough to dispatch soldiers quickly toward either the Linzhao border to the east or the Chengfeng border to the north. Flags fly openly at the camp's gate, visible from the road. Drill here is real and frequent, not ceremonial; Suwei Ying's soldiers are regularly called out against bandits operating somewhere within Ningyao itself, and the camp carries the look of a force that actually uses its training.
Zhenhai Camp.hiddenInfo: Zhenhai Camp runs on Xie Yanzhao's coin far more than House Yongtai's — supply, wages, and equipment here trace back to funding the Crown Prince quietly arranges himself, not the Palace's own allocation. Long-serving soldiers know this without ever discussing it openly; newer recruits simply absorb it as how things work. The camp's real strength is genuine: regular bandit engagements have made these soldiers battle-tested in a way most of House Yongtai's forces are not, though no one here has ever measured that experience against a real army. The bandits themselves remain a loose end — their camp is somewhere inside Ningyao, never yet located, an ongoing operational frustration rather than a solved problem.

Ningyao-Linzhao Border.name: Ningyao-Linzhao Border
Ningyao-Linzhao Border.basicInfo: The road east from Ningyao toward Linzhao, where flat river-mouth farmland gradually gives way to Linzhao's rockier, harbor-cut coastline. The garrisoned checkpoint sits on the last stretch of solid coastal road, on a headland just before the route drops into Linzhao's harbor district proper. Traffic here is steady and mundane — traders, travelers, and the occasional stranger passing between the two circuits — with little cause for real concern in either direction.
Ningyao-Linzhao Border.hiddenInfo: Some of the funding and supply Xie Yanzhao quietly arranges for Suwei Ying moves through here — disguised as ordinary trade, easy to lose among Linzhao's usual traffic of strangers and shipments. The soldiers manning this post don't know the full picture; they simply wave certain shipments through on standing orders, never questioning why.

Ningyao-Chengfeng Border.name: Ningyao-Chengfeng Border
Ningyao-Chengfeng Border.basicInfo: The road north from Ningyao toward Chengfeng, where mild coastal farmland begins climbing into cooler, sparser highland. A garrisoned checkpoint marks the crossing, staffed by soldiers dispatched from Zhenhai Camp. Traffic thins noticeably compared to the Linzhao road — fewer travelers, fewer reasons to pass through, and a colder wind that makes itself known well before the true highlands start.
Ningyao-Chengfeng Border.hiddenInfo: A handful of travelers have gone missing crossing toward Chengfeng over the past year — enough that locals have started avoiding the road after dark, and rumors have crept in about something unnatural in the highland treeline. The truth is more mundane: a large northern predator has been drawn down by easy prey along the route, opportunistic rather than territorial, and entirely unrelated to anything Suwei Ying or House Yongtai is doing. No one's confirmed this yet — the patrol here treats the disappearances as unsolved, and the rumors have only grown louder for it.

Guixiang Hui Camp.name: Guixiang Hui Camp
Guixiang Hui Camp.basicInfo: A hidden camp somewhere in Ningyao's western reaches, closer to the highland approach toward Chengfeng than to Zhenhai Camp itself. Deliberately unremarkable from any distance — no fires visible by day, no fixed structures worth noticing from the road. Whatever exists here is built to be abandoned quickly, not defended.
Guixiang Hui Camp.hiddenInfo:
Home to what remains of Ningyao's displaced original population — Guixiang Hui's actual base, never yet located by Suwei Ying or House Yongtai. Its position is deliberate: far enough from Zhenhai Camp and the main roads that any real reinforcement would have to pass through the camp first, giving Guixiang Hui warning and room to scatter before help ever arrives. Life here is sparse and precarious, held together more by shared grievance and memory of what Ningyao was than by any real military organization. They know they can't win a real fight — survival depends entirely on never being found.

Among the camp's modest stores of looted goods sits Chen Wanru's Pipa — sandalwood body, a plum-blossom inlay, a worn nick near the soundhole, finer than anything else here. Guixiang Hui has no idea what it actually is or who it belonged to; it was taken in a raid some time ago along with everything else of value, and sits unremarked among their things. Its real significance — that it belonged to House Jiangyuan's Lu Zhengting's late wife, and that he has been quietly searching for it ever since — is completely unknown to them.

Hegang.name: Hegang
Hegang.basicInfo: Hegang is a trade town in Ningyao, sitting along the road that leads toward the Ningyao-Linzhao border crossing — the last real settlement travelers pass before reaching it. Warehouses, porters, and merchants move goods here between the circuit's farmland and Linzhao's harbors beyond. Labor is constant and visible: loading, hauling, sorting, much of it performed by servants and laborers bound to the merchant houses and estates that run Hegang's trade, a normal enough sight that few visitors think twice about it.
Hegang.hiddenInfo: Some of Xie Yanzhao's off-the-books funding for Suwei Ying moves through Hegang before reaching the border crossing — folded into ordinary trade shipments, easy to lose among the town's usual volume of goods and porters. The merchant houses handling it don't necessarily know what they're actually moving, only that certain shipments come with instructions not to ask questions. Separately, Hegang's servants and bound laborers are drawn overwhelmingly from families descended from Ningyao's original population — the same lineage Guixiang Hui comes from — though few in the town think of it that way anymore. Resentment here runs quiet rather than open: no organized defiance, just old grievance worn down into daily endurance.

Tunzi.name: Tunzi
Tunzi.basicInfo: Tunzi is a small village in Ningyao that grew up around Zhenhai Camp itself — soldiers' families, camp followers, and the small trades that naturally cluster around a working garrison: mending, provisioning, brewing, lodging for visiting kin. Life here moves to the camp's rhythm more than the season's; drills, dispatches, and changing patrols are as much a part of daily routine as farm work is elsewhere in Ningyao.
Tunzi.hiddenInfo: A handful of Tunzi's families quietly have kin among Guixiang Hui — not fighters themselves, but relatives who chose to stay, work, and survive rather than flee to the hills. Nobody speaks of it openly, and no one in Tunzi would call it disloyalty; it's simply not discussed. If it ever became a matter of real suspicion, more than one household here would have something to hide.

Heyu.name: Heyu
Heyu.basicInfo: Heyu is a farming and fishing village to the south of Ningyao, where the Suining River's reach into paddies and fish ponds is most directly felt. Life here moves with the seasons and the tides in equal measure — planting and harvest on one hand, netting and pond-tending on the other. Quieter and further from the road than Ningyao's other settlements, with little reason for outsiders to pass through.
Heyu.hiddenInfo: Heyu produces more fish and rice than it can use, and has for years — but there's no real market for it. Everyone nearby grows or catches the same things, outside merchants barely know the village exists, and the ones who do rarely think the isolated road here is worth the trouble, especially with Guixiang Hui's activity making travelers wary of Ningyao's back roads in general. The result is a village sitting on real surplus with nowhere to sell it — a problem no one in Heyu has the means or connections to solve themselves.

Yizhan.name: Yizhan
Yizhan.basicInfo: Yizhan is a waypoint town in Huicheng, sitting along the main road between Wanhua and Ningyao — a natural stopping point for travelers, merchants, and couriers moving between the capital and the coast. Inns, stables, and modest trade line the road through town, busy enough to feel alive but without any single industry or institution defining it.

Tianxiang.name: Tianxiang
Tianxiang.basicInfo: Tianxiang is a market town in Yufeng, built around the orchard trade that defines the region — fruit stalls, cider presses, and drying racks are as much a part of the town's daily rhythm as any formal market. Less trafficked than the river towns of Fumin or Wanhua, but steady and self-sufficient, with a reputation among nearby circuits for the quality of what it grows.

Wanqiao.name: Wanqiao
Wanqiao.basicInfo: Wanqiao is a town in Fumin built entirely around the great bridge its name comes from — House Jiangyuan's ancestral crossing over the Suining River, connecting House Yongtai's land upstream to the South's territory beyond. Warehouses, toll offices, and inns cluster at both ends of the span, and the bridge itself is constantly in use: grain barges passing beneath it, travelers and merchants queuing to cross above. Nothing moves through Wanqiao without paying House Jiangyuan's price, in silver or in goods — a rule that applies to everyone equally, House Yongtai included.
Wanqiao.hiddenInfo: Wanqiao's toll gates are the physical enforcement of House Jiangyuan's arrangement with House Yongtai — grain tax already covers House Yongtai's own passage, but every other party pays in silver or resources, no exceptions made for status. What isn't advertised is the bridge's other function: it would close instantly and without negotiation to any force marching against the West, House Jiangyuan's real ally. The toll keepers who work the gates don't know the full political weight of what they're guarding — to them, it's simply the rule, enforced the same way every day.

Fengcang.name: Fengcang
Fengcang.basicInfo: Fengcang is a granary town in Fumin, on House Yongtai's side of the Suining River, where the circuit's grain surplus is gathered and stored before moving downstream toward the capital or across the river through Wanqiao's toll. Warehouses and threshing yards dominate the town's layout, and its granaries are kept deliberately full — the monthly tax that buys House Yongtai's passage across House Jiangyuan's bridge is paid from here.

Tiexue Camp.name: Tiexue Camp
Tiexue Camp.basicInfo: Tiexue Camp is House Beiying's forward garrison at the Hanfeng frontier, a sprawling, standardized military encampment built for sustained pressure rather than a single decisive push. Rows of drilling grounds, supply lines, and rotating companies reflect House Beiying's real advantage: depth, numbers, and discipline that can simply be replaced when worn down. Flags fly openly here — Tiexue Camp has nothing to hide and no reason to.
Tiexue Camp.hiddenInfo: Despite years of pressure, Tiexue Camp's own veteran officers privately know their advance has stalled for reasons no amount of additional strength has fixed — sudden windstorms that erase visibility without warning, and ground that looks uniform but conceals firm paths and treacherous soft stretches only Hanfeng's own defenders seem able to read. It's cost real losses, quietly written off as the price of frontier war rather than examined as a pattern. A commander who actually solved this, rather than simply pushing harder, would be doing something no one here has managed in years.

Fengbi Camp.name: Fengbi Camp
Fengbi Camp.basicInfo: Fengbi Camp is House Xiling's defensive anchor on the Hanfeng frontier, built low and dug into the land itself rather than sprawling outward — fewer soldiers than House Beiying fields, but positioned with total familiarity of the ground they defend. The camp takes its name from the sudden windstorms that sweep this stretch of frontier, which Xiling's own soldiers read and use as naturally as breathing.
Fengbi Camp.hiddenInfo: Fengbi Camp's entire defense rests on knowledge that can't be trained into an outsider quickly — which stretches of ground hold firm underfoot and which don't, when a windstorm is building versus when it's just weather, how to use zero visibility offensively rather than defensively. This is genuinely working, but it's also entirely dependent on Hanfeng's own veterans, most of whom have been fighting this exact stretch of frontier for years; losing enough of them at once, faster than new defenders can actually learn the land, is the one scenario nobody at Fengbi Camp says out loud.

Houying.name: Houying
Houying.basicInfo: Houying is House Beiying's staging ground just behind the Hanfeng frontier, built entirely around keeping Tiexue Camp supplied and reinforced. Depots, wagon yards, and rotating barracks dominate the town, and the road toward the frontier stays busy in both directions — fresh soldiers and supplies moving forward, the wounded and worn-down moving back. Life here runs on the war's rhythm more than any season's.
Houying.hiddenInfo: Houying sees House Beiying's frontier losses more honestly than anywhere else in the North — the wounded who pass through here, and the supply requisitions that never quite match what Tiexue Camp officially reports needing, tell a quieter story than the confident dispatches sent back to Zhenbei Hall. Nobody here is hiding anything deliberately; it's simply the place where the real cost of holding Hanfeng is most visible, to anyone who bothers to actually look at what moves through instead of what's said about it.

Zhenbei Hall.name: Zhenbei Hall
Zhenbei Hall.basicInfo: Zhenbei Hall is House Beiying's seat, the true center of the North's power — not a frontier post, but where the house actually rules from. Set in Guandao's warm lowland corridor, far enough from Hanfeng's cold and constant war footing to feel like a different world entirely. Administration, ceremony, and the house's real wealth all move through here, and its presence alone marks Guandao as the North's true population and political center.
Zhenbei Hall.hiddenInfo: Zhenbei Hall runs the North's war at a comfortable remove — real decisions about Hanfeng are made here, by people who've mostly never stood on that frontier themselves. Marshal Han Boqing, who built House Beiying's unity in his own lifetime, sees this clearly and pushes back on it constantly — but his court increasingly overrules him, trusting sanitized written reports over the judgment of a man who fought real war himself, decades ago. His three daughters, Han Yuwei, Han Suqing, and Han Xiaoyue, are each genuinely capable, but the court gives none of them the standing it would give a son — the real reason command at Tiexue Camp still belongs to Meng Zhanhu rather than any of them.

Zhenbei Cheng.name: Zhenbei Cheng
Zhenbei Cheng.basicInfo: Zhenbei Cheng grew outward from Zhenbei Hall itself, over years, until hall and city became inseparable — House Beiying's true capital in practice as well as name. Most men here pass through military service at some point in their lives, whether taken young or later, and the city's rhythm still bears the shape of that: drilling grounds, barracks, and veterans' quarters woven throughout what's otherwise an ordinary, populous capital.
Zhenbei Cheng.hiddenInfo: Zhenbei Cheng's male population has been quietly thinning for years, a slow demographic drain from generations of sustained military service and the losses that come with it — nothing dramatic enough for the court to have noticed or addressed, since it shows up gradually in daily life long before it would ever appear as a number worth acting on. Ordinary residents have started to notice it themselves, though — a street with fewer young men than it used to have, a household with more daughters raised than sons who stayed. It's talked about quietly, among people who live it, not yet as a real political concern.

Liuguang Border.name: Liuguang Border
Liuguang Border.basicInfo: The northernmost checkpoint overlooking Sanjie Huang, planted by House Beiying generations ago at the closest possible line to the wilderness pocket shared uneasily with Chengfeng and Dongrui. A real garrisoned outpost rather than a lone watchtower — walls, quarters, a proper gate — Han Xiaoyue's men patrol here in shifts, watching land that belongs to no one and answers to nothing. The cold bites harder here than in Liuguang proper, and the wilderness beyond stays largely unmapped.
Liuguang Border.hiddenInfo: House Beiying's border here has never moved since it was first planted — a mark of old strength more than current necessity, since relations with both Chengfeng and Dongrui have long since eased. No one has suggested pulling it back, or pushing it forward; House Beiying's own reputation alone has kept anyone from testing the line in either direction. The soldiers stationed here mostly patrol boredom and weather rather than any real threat — Sanjie Huang has never produced anything more dangerous than the occasional lost traveler or wild animal, though no one's ever mapped it properly enough to say that with total confidence.

Xiling Fu.name: Xiling Fu
Xiling Fu.basicInfo: Xiling Fu is House Xiling's seat, set high on Jinshan's gold-bearing plateau rather than anywhere more comfortable — thin air, extreme swings between scorching day and freezing night, the same demanding ground its own miners and herders live on. Mining wealth and herding trade both pass through here before moving anywhere else, and the hall itself is built practical and sturdy against the climate, not for display. There's a rougher, more grounded character to ruling from here than the ease House Beiying's own capital enjoys.
Xiling Fu.hiddenInfo: Xiling Fu's leadership doesn't have Zhenbei Hall's luxury of distance — reports from Fengbi Camp reach Marshal Bai Suyin fast, and anyone who's spent real time on this plateau already understands what the frontier costs without needing to be told. Whatever complacency exists in House Beiying's court has no real equivalent here; Jinshan's own climate won't allow it.

Jinshan Gold Mine.name: Jinshan Gold Mine
Jinshan Gold Mine.basicInfo: Jinshan Gold Mine is the largest of several mining sites worked into Jinshan's plateau slopes, operating under House Xiling's authority. Anyone from Jinshan, or any outsider willing to travel this far, can work here — locals and strangers alike, so long as they carry no grievance against House Xiling. Equipment is provided, safety is taken seriously, and every miner reports their output honestly in exchange for a fair wage and real compensation should the worst happen to their family. Life here is hard, physical, and unglamorous, but genuinely fair by the standards of this kind of work.
Jinshan Gold Mine.hiddenInfo: Nothing genuinely hidden here — the mine runs largely as it appears: honest labor, honest wages, a rare kind of institutional fairness for a place this remote and difficult. House Xiling's willingness to compensate families generously for real losses has earned real loyalty here, the kind that isn't bought so much as genuinely deserved.

Yufeng-Chengjin Border.name: Yufeng-Chengjin Border
Yufeng-Chengjin Border.basicInfo: The road west from Yufeng toward Chengjin, where orchard country gradually gives way to rockier, higher ground at the edge of House Xiling's territory. A garrisoned checkpoint marks House Yongtai's side of the crossing — walls, a gate, quarters for the soldiers stationed here — and travelers move through steadily in both directions, drawn by Chengjin's gold trade, though nothing of real material value crosses the border itself beyond what a traveler carries personally.
Yufeng-Chengjin Border.hiddenInfo: Nothing genuinely hidden here — House Yongtai and House Xiling have no real relationship to speak of, cordial or otherwise, and this crossing reflects that: functional, unremarkable, watched more out of habit than any actual concern. Traders headed to Chengjin pass through constantly; nothing resembling a formal resource arrangement between the two houses has ever existed here, or is expected to.

Fengrong Yuan.name: Fengrong Yuan
Fengrong Yuan.basicInfo: Fengrong Yuan is House Fengrong's private estate, set apart from Fengdu's public bustle — where the house actually conducts its real business, away from the market's noise and eyes. Fine but understated, wealth shown through quality rather than display; House Fengrong has never needed to prove anything with ornamentation when its influence already speaks for itself.
Fengrong Yuan.hiddenInfo: This is where House Fengrong's real leverage gets managed — quiet conversations, favors called in, debts acknowledged without ever being written down. Nothing here looks dramatic from the outside, which is exactly the point; the house's actual power moves through rooms like this one, not through anything anyone could point to as proof.

Fengdu.name: Fengdu
Fengdu.basicInfo: Fengdu is the South's true capital in practice if not yet fully in name — a genuine city that grew around the wealth passing through Fengmu's markets, now home to more people, more houses, and more real political weight than anywhere else in the South. House Fengrong doesn't rule it outright the way House Yongtai rules Wanhua, but no other house disputes that Fengdu is where the South's real business happens.
Fengdu.hiddenInfo: Fengdu's informal status as "capital" is a source of quiet tension nobody voices directly — other Southern houses benefit too much from the city's trade to openly resent House Fengrong's outsized influence here, but the arrangement has never been formalized, and everyone privately understands that could change if House Fengrong's position ever weakened.

Fengshi.name: Fengshi
Fengshi.basicInfo: Fengshi is the largest livestock market in Qianzhou, drawing merchants, herders, and buyers from every circuit willing to make the trip. Cattle, sheep, and horses change hands here by the thousands each season, alongside everything that naturally clusters around trade at this scale — moneylenders, brokers, scribes for contracts, inns for those staying to bargain properly.
Fengshi.hiddenInfo: Fengshi is where House Fengrong's real leverage actually gets built, turn by turn — every major deal here creates a debt, a favor, or a dependency somewhere, and the house's people watch closely enough to know exactly who owes what to whom. Nothing about the market itself looks political; that's precisely how it accumulates real power without ever needing to look for it directly.

Baicao Zhuang.name: Baicao Zhuang
Baicao Zhuang.basicInfo: Baicao Zhuang sits at the edge of Tiefeng's forest, close enough to the plants that give the settlement its purpose to gather what's needed without real difficulty. A working herbalist village on its surface — drying racks, processing sheds, physicians training apprentices — genuinely respected across the South and beyond for the quality of what it produces. Generations old, established back when the Center itself still knew war firsthand.
Baicao Zhuang.hiddenInfo: What looks like an ordinary, if unusually skilled, herbalist village is also where House Baicao's real knowledge actually lives — the antidotes, the slow poisons, the methods no one outside the family has ever been taught. Nothing here advertises that truth; the same buildings and the same people serve both purposes, and only someone who already knows what to look for would ever suspect there's more happening than medicine.

Wanhua Park.name: Wanhua Park
Wanhua Park.basicInfo:
A landscaped riverside park southwest of Yongtai Palace, connected to the West Residential District by a footbridge over the Suining. Winding paths, ornamental plantings, and quiet pavilions make it Wanhua's favored spot for a walk, a private conversation, or simply escaping the noise of the Market District nearby.

Yinlu Hua, a small pale flower with a faint dew-like sheen, grows throughout the Park in real abundance — common enough that locals long ago gave it its own name, and children string it into garlands.
Wanhua Park.hiddenInfo: Roughly one in a hundred Yinlu Hua growing in the Park is actually a distinct, visually identical sibling species, Yueying Hua — indistinguishable except by a children's game: soaking a picked flower in salt water causes only the rare sibling to slowly change color. Most who still play the game as adults treat it as nostalgic superstition, not botany, and no one in Wanhua has ever connected it to anything of real value.

Tingfeng Zhuang.name: Tingfeng Zhuang
Tingfeng Zhuang.basicInfo: Tingfeng Zhuang is a modest, private compound in Fengmu, home to Xuedi Men. Unremarkable from the outside — plain walls, a working courtyard, nothing that suggests the history behind the name of the house that lives there. Rarely visited, rarely discussed; most in Fengmu who know of it have no real reason to go looking, and Xuedi Men has never given anyone cause to.
Tingfeng Zhuang.hiddenInfo: Life inside Tingfeng Zhuang is genuinely quiet — training, simple routine, generations of the same discipline passed down without ceremony. Nothing here looks like a threat because it almost never needs to be one; the compound's real defense is the story attached to its name, not anything visible within its walls. Should that ever change, everyone in Fengmu already understands what they'd be dealing with.

Baiwan Gang.name: Baiwan Gang
Baiwan Gang.basicInfo: Baiwan Gang is Muyu's largest port town, sprawling across a knot of inlets on the mainland coast directly opposite Guyu Island. No single house or family rules here — merchant houses from half a dozen other circuits keep offices and warehouses side by side, each bringing their own hired labor and property guards, while local administrators handle the town's actual civic functions. Foreign traders are a common sight, some with real local ties built over years, others here purely for business and gone within the season.
Baiwan Gang.hiddenInfo: Baiwan Gang's lack of a single ruling power isn't an oversight — no outside house has ever managed to hold it, given how quickly the others unite in temporary alliance against anyone who tries. What actually keeps the peace is mutual dependency: every merchant house here needs the harbor functioning smoothly more than it wants to control it outright. Newer arrivals, foreign and local alike, without established ties to any of the existing merchant houses are genuinely vulnerable here — protection has to be earned or bought, and the town offers neither for free.

Guyu Island.name: Guyu Island
Guyu Island.basicInfo: Guyu Island sits offshore from Muyu's mainland coast, visible from Baiwan Gang on a clear day — a large landmass that is, in practice, foreign soil within Qianzhou's own waters. No single power holds it: Amakuni, Torgastan, and Esterlund have each established real, substantial footholds here over generations, none strong enough to push the others off the island entirely, and none willing to risk open war against several rivals at once to try. Significant stretches of land remain unclaimed even now — genuinely usable ground, not scraps, sitting between the established territories.
Guyu Island.hiddenInfo: House Yongtai has wanted Guyu Island for generations, and has never once had the military strength to actually take it — the same weakness quietly underlying the Center's whole military reputation. The island itself is the real prize: its size, its harbors, its position, all make it a genuine foundation for building real power from nothing — a trade empire, a fleet, an entire nation's foothold, whatever someone with the ambition and means could actually build here. Every established foreign claim on the island understands exactly how valuable the remaining unclaimed land is, and every one of them would rather see it stay unclaimed than let a rival — foreign or Qianzhou-born — take it outright. That standoff, more than anything else, is what's kept the island from ever being fully divided.
